thumbnail.analysis: Actual 1280x720 and 320x180 inspected. White field; left a sweating, wide-eyed, open-mouthed cartoon man in a gray T-shirt; right a grid chart with a thick red zigzag line falling to a large downward arrow; heavy black "IT STARTED..." with ellipsis and small curved arrow. Mobile: text and crash arrow highly legible. Image is an unspecified crisis/alarm cue with no bond or rate reference; together with the educational title it pairs fear ("it started") with a knowledge promise. Script does discuss real bond-driven crises (2022, SVB, gilts), so alarm is partially supported but the image's implied imminent crash is not the script's thesis.

script.opening_words:
Last month, a guy in Ohio sat down at a
closing table to sign a mortgage.
30-year fixed 6.6%.
He asked the loan officer a simple
question, "Who decided 6.6?" And the
loan officer gave him the corporate
smile and said, "That's just where rates
are right now." That's not an answer.
That's a shrug with a lanyard. So,
here's the actual answer. That number
wasn't picked by his bank. It wasn't
picked by the Fed. It was set by a
market most people have
script.ending_words:

days, and trillions in safe retirement
money. None of those people thought
bonds were boring afterward. You don't

finance degree. You just need to stop
being the only person at the table who
doesn't know what that 6.6%

to keep pricing your life either way.
The only question is whether you can

made you think I could make videos like

link is in the description. I'll see you
in the next one.
script.analysis: All 18,811 stored characters read in two contiguous ranges with canonical hash match. Cold open: Ohio borrower asks who set his 6.6% mortgage rate; global bond market (~$145T) framed as invisible pricing machine; subscribe CTA with humor. Mechanics: bond as IOU, coupon/maturity, treasuries/corporates/junk; worked 2%-to-5% price example ("somewhere in the 700s"); rule "rates up, prices down". 10-year Treasury as key rate, mortgage spread, 2021 lows to 2023 highs, refinancing and layoffs, inverted yield curve record, Carville quote; like CTA. 2022: Fed hikes, Aggregate -13%, long zero-coupon -39.2% (worst since 1754), 60/40 -17%; duration explained. Dominoes: SVB, UK gilt/LDI crisis and Truss, Austria 2120 bond and negative-yield era. US debt ~$39T, >$1T interest, Moody's 2025 downgrade, foreign share decline, April 2025 tariff pause. Mid-late "school community" CTA teaching video-making. Action list: T-bills/money funds vs 0.5% savings, bond vs bond fund, duration, I bonds/TIPS, watch the 10-year; disclaimer; close callback to 6.6% and community link. Tight escalating structure with concrete historical stories, humor and a practical payoff - one of the channel's strongest scripts in craft and sourcing, though a few figures are imprecise. ASR errors ("Series 1" for Series I, "in 2021" for 2120) preserved; not audio-verified.

claim_audit: 0:9500 $1,000 2% bond repriced to a 5% market yield with ~9 years left = ~$787, consistent with "somewhere in the 700s"; the script says the $20 coupon "works out to roughly 5%", but the 5% is yield-to-maturity including price accretion (current yield ~2.5%). Global bond market ~$145T exceeding global equity capitalization is consistent with SIFMA-type estimates (~$140T+). Mortgage 2.65% record low (Jan 2021) and ~19% one-year home-price gains consistent with Freddie Mac/FHFA history. "Mortgages crossed 8% by late 2023": Freddie Mac PMMS peaked ~7.79% (Oct 2023), while some daily indexes topped 8% - source-dependent. Inverted curve preceding recessions since 1955 with one 1960s false signal matches SF Fed research.

0:9500 2022: Fed funds from near zero to over 4% by December (~9 months) correct; Bloomberg US Aggregate ~-13% and worst since 1976 correct; long zero-coupon Treasuries ~-39% and "worst since 1754" consistent with McQuarrie's historical series as publicized; 60/40 ~-16 to -17% consistent. "Rates rose more than four points" applies to the policy rate; 10-year and long Treasury yields rose roughly 2.5-3 points in 2022, so the duration-17 example overstates if applied to long yields. Duration rule of thumb correctly explained.

9500:18811 SVB ~$91B held-to-maturity securities, ~$15B unrealized losses, $1.8B realized loss and ~48-hour failure consistent with Fed/FDIC reviews. UK: ~£45B unfunded tax cuts, 30-year gilt yields up >1 point within days, BoE emergency purchases, Truss resignation after ~45 days (shortest premiership) and lettuce livestream all consistent with public record. Austria 0.85% 2120 bond (2020) and ~75% peak-to-trough loss consistent; ~$18T negative-yielding debt peak (late 2020) consistent.

9500:18811 US debt ~$39T (mid-2026) plausible; net interest >$1T and above defense consistent with CBO projections; "second biggest line item behind Social Security" depends on whether Medicare is counted net. Moody's May 2025 downgrade ending the last top US rating correct. Foreign share of Treasuries from ~half (2008) to ~30% approximately consistent with Treasury TIC data; April 2025 tariff pause with presidential "queasy" remark consistent with reporting. T-bill interest exempt from state income tax correct; savings ~0.5% vs T-bills ~3.7% "eight times" roughly consistent. I bond 9.62% (May-Oct 2022) correct; current ~4.3% unverified.

Less saturated on this channel than spending/frugality topics.
